title: Sea days are not filler. They are the design.
subtitle: Where a sea day sits in the week decides whether you come home rested.

text: Four port days in a row isn't an itinerary. It's a commute.
sub: Consecutive port days each begin at the gangway and end against a clock. By the third, most travellers go ashore out of obligation rather than appetite.

points.label: Days 1 - 2
points.value: Embarkation, then a sea day. You arrive on the ship before you arrive anywhere.

points.label: Day 3
points.value: First port, alongside at 08:00. Rested enough to actually want it.

points.label: Day 4
points.value: Second port, overnight. The evening the voyage gets remembered for.

points.label: Day 5
points.value: Sea day, mid-week. The one that makes days six and seven possible.

points.label: Days 6 - 7
points.value: Final port, then a slow morning into the disembarkation city.

items.head: The sea day parked on day two
items.body: Placed where it reads well in a brochure, before anyone needs it. A waste of the best day of the week.

items.head: Four consecutive port calls
items.body: Each one costs an early start. Enjoyment falls off after the second; attendance, unfortunately, does not.

items.head: A dawn arrival after a late sailing
items.body: Away at eight in the evening, anchored at seven the next morning. Nobody sleeps and the day pays for it.

quote: A sea day placed properly is the most valuable day on the ship. Placed badly, it's the one people apologise for.

title: Send me the week and I'll re-order it.
body: Same ports, better sequence, and often the same fare. Tell me which sailing you're looking at and I'll show you the version that reads calmer.
